title: The Way That Seems Right
excerpt: Proverbs says it twice: there is a way that seems right but leads to death. Why our own certainty isn't a safe guide, and who is.

blocks.text: Here's something odd about the book of Proverbs.

It is a book made of short, sharp sayings, hundreds of them, each one a different angle on how to live well. Nothing is wasted. There's no filler. And yet, if you read carefully, you'll find one sentence that appears twice, word for word, eleven chapters apart:

verses: There is a way that appears to be right, but in the end it leads to death.

blocks.text: The writer of Proverbs wasn't running out of material. When a book that compact repeats itself exactly, it's worth stopping to ask why. What did he want us to notice so badly that he said it twice?
I think the answer is hiding in a single word: *appears*.
The Most Convincing Voice You'll Ever Hear

Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't warn about the way that looks wrong, or feels wrong, or comes with a flashing sign. We don't need Proverbs for that. We already know to avoid the obviously bad path.

The danger it points to is the path that looks *right*. It makes sense. It feels justified. It has reasons, and the reasons are good ones. And the voice recommending it is the most persuasive voice in your life: your own.

Proverbs comes back to this over and over. "A person may think their own ways are right, but the LORD weighs the heart" (21:2). "Those who trust in themselves are fools" (28:26). Strong words, but the point isn't that you're stupid. It's that your sense of certainty isn't a reliable measure of whether you're correct. Feeling sure and being right are two different things, and from the inside they feel exactly the same.

Think of the last time you made a decision you later regretted. Chances are, at the time, you had your reasons. You weren't being reckless. You'd talked yourself into it, step by logical step. Maybe you were even praying about it, and the "peace" you felt was really just the relief of getting the answer you wanted.
Sincerity is not the same as safety. History has plenty of examples, but my favorite is also the most uncomfortable.
A Man Who Was Absolutely Certain

Before he was the apostle Paul, he was Saul of Tarsus, and he was passionate. He'd studied Scripture his whole life. He was zealous for God. And he was fully convinced that the new Jesus movement was a dangerous heresy that needed to be stopped. So he hunted down believers and approved of their deaths.
Years later, looking back, he says something chilling: "I too was convinced that I ought to do all that was possible to oppose the name of Jesus" (Acts 26:9).

*Convinced.* Not confused. Not conflicted. Saul wasn't a man struggling with doubt who chose evil anyway. He was a man with total clarity, moving in total sincerity, in exactly the wrong direction. If anyone ever had a way that seemed right, he did. He wasn't lacking zeal. He was lacking sight, and he couldn't see it until the light on the Damascus road knocked him to the ground.
That should humble all of us. It means that the strength of your conviction can't be the only thing you check. A person can be sure and still be walking toward the wrong thing.
So What Do We Do With That?
If we can't fully trust our own sense of "this feels right," how are we supposed to live? Proverbs doesn't leave us hanging.

verses: Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.

blocks.text: This verse is so familiar it can slide past without landing, and it's often misread as "don't think" or "turn off your brain." That isn't the point. God gave you a mind, and He expects you to use it. The point is about where your final trust sits. Your understanding is a tool, not a throne. It's useful, but it's limited, and it can be wrong without telling you.

Notice, too, the posture in the second half: *submit*. Submit to Him in all your ways. That's a hard word in a culture that prizes self-determination. But here it isn't a loss. It's a promise. Do that, and He will make your paths straight. He doesn't promise a path with no hills, only one that actually gets you where you were meant to go.
Alongside that, Proverbs gives some very practical guardrails for decisions:

**Hold your plans loosely.** "In their hearts humans plan their course, but the LORD establishes their steps" (16:9). Planning is good. Gripping is the problem. The wisest plans leave room for God to say something different.

**Welcome counsel, especially the uncomfortable kind.** "The way of fools seems right to them, but the wise listen to advice" (12:15). Notice the echo of that repeated phrase, *seems right*. The mark of a fool here isn't a lack of intelligence. It's the inability to hear a second opinion. If you have a decision you're very sure about, and you're reluctant to run it past anyone you trust, that reluctance is information.

**Check it against what God has already said.** The final verse of the book of Judges has a haunting line about a time when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (21:25). The result wasn't freedom. It was chaos. God's Word isn't there to limit us. It's a fixed point outside ourselves, something our own certainty can't bend.
The Answer Isn't a Method

Here's what I love about the way the Bible lands this. It would be easy to walk away from a passage like this with a checklist: seek counsel, test your motives, read your Bible. All good things. But a checklist can only get you so far, because the real problem is that we can't see our own blind spots, and we need more than a better technique.
What we need is someone who can see what we can't, and who will actually walk with us.

Jesus said something that, in this context, hits differently: "I am the way and the truth and the life" (John 14:6). He didn't say, "I'll show you the way." He didn't say, "I'll give you better directions." He said, *I am the way.* The answer to every path that only appears right is a person, not a plan.

And He modeled it. In the garden, the night before the cross, facing the hardest decision any person has ever faced, He prayed, "Not my will, but yours be done" (Luke 22:42). Perfect wisdom, and yet He still submitted. If the Son of God laid down His own preferences to follow the Father, we can stop pretending our own are reliable enough to trust alone.
A Question Worth Asking This Week
Is there something in your life you feel really sure about right now? A decision, a direction, a grievance, a relationship? Something where you've already made up your mind?

Don't panic. Being sure isn't a sin. But ask yourself the question Proverbs is pressing on you: *Have I actually handed this to God, or have I just decided and asked Him to agree?* Talk to someone wise. Open the Word. Sit still long enough to hear something you might not like.
The way that seems right is dangerous precisely because it feels so safe. Don't trust the feeling. Trust the One who knows where every road actually ends.

Lord, You see what I can't. Forgive me for the times I've leaned on my own understanding and called it wisdom. Show me where I'm certain and wrong. Give me the humility to listen, the courage to submit, and the faith to follow You even when my own path seems clearer. Be my way. Amen.
